amc10-2011-10a-01.title: Work in cents
amc10-2011-10a-01.body:
Everything in cents: $2000 + 100\cdot 5 + 30\cdot 10 = 2000+500+300 = 2800$ cents, which is \$28.00.

**Answer: (D) \$28.00**

amc10-2011-10a-02.title: Divide and round up
amc10-2011-10a-02.body:
$500\div 35 = 14\frac{2}{7}$. Fourteen small bottles hold only $14\cdot 35=490$ mL, which is not enough, so she needs $15$ bottles ($525$ mL).

**Answer: (E) 15**

amc10-2011-10a-02.title: Check the choices
amc10-2011-10a-02.body:
$14\cdot 35 = 490<500$ and $15\cdot 35=525\ge 500$, so $15$ is the least number that works.

**Answer: (E) 15**

amc10-2011-10a-03.title: Weights
amc10-2011-10a-03.body:
The outer average gives each of its three entries weight $\frac13$. The inner averages split that further: the numbers $1,1,0$ each get weight $\frac19$ and $0,1$ each get $\frac16$. So the value is $\frac19+\frac19+\frac16 = \frac{4+3}{18}=\frac{7}{18}$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac{7}{18}$**

amc10-2011-10a-04.title: Pair up terms
amc10-2011-10a-04.body:
Both sums have $\frac{100-10}{2}+1 = 46$ terms. Each term of $Y$ is $2$ more than the matching term of $X$, so $Y-X = 46\cdot 2 = 92$.

**Answer: (A) 92**

amc10-2011-10a-04.title: Cancel the common part
amc10-2011-10a-04.body:
The terms $12+14+\dots+100$ appear in both sums and cancel. What is left is $Y-X = 102-10=92$.

**Answer: (A) 92**

amc10-2011-10a-05.title: Choose a convenient count
amc10-2011-10a-05.body:
Say there is $1$ fifth grader, so $2$ fourth graders and $4$ third graders ($7$ students). Total minutes: $4\cdot 12 + 2\cdot 15 + 1\cdot 10 = 48+30+10=88$. Average: $\frac{88}{7}$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{88}{7}$**

amc10-2011-10a-05.title: Weighted average with variables
amc10-2011-10a-05.body:
With $f$ fifth graders there are $2f$ fourth and $4f$ third graders. Average $=\frac{12\cdot 4f+15\cdot 2f+10f}{7f}=\frac{88f}{7f}=\frac{88}{7}$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{88}{7}$**

amc10-2011-10a-06.title: Make the overlap as large as possible
amc10-2011-10a-06.body:
The union contains all of $A$, so it has at least $20$ elements. If every element of $B$ is also in $A$ (that is, $B\subseteq A$), the union is exactly $A$, with $20$ elements.

**Answer: (C) 20**

amc10-2011-10a-06.title: Inclusion–exclusion
amc10-2011-10a-06.body:
$|A\cup B| = 20+15-|A\cap B|$. The intersection has at most $15$ elements, so the union has at least $35-15=20$ elements, attained when $B\subseteq A$.

**Answer: (C) 20**

amc10-2011-10a-07.title: Check each equation
amc10-2011-10a-07.body:
- (A) $x=-7$ works.
- (B) $|-3x|+5\ge 5>0$, so it is never $0$: no solution.
- (C) $\sqrt{-x}=2$ gives $x=-4$.
- (D) $\sqrt x = 8$ gives $x=64$.
- (E) $|-3x|=4$ gives $x=\pm\frac43$.

**Answer: (B)**

amc10-2011-10a-07.title: Absolute values are never negative
amc10-2011-10a-07.body:
Equation (B) says $|-3x| = -5$. An absolute value can never be negative, so (B) has no solution. (The others can each be solved directly.)

**Answer: (B)**

amc10-2011-10a-08.title: Imagine 100 birds
amc10-2011-10a-08.body:
With $100$ birds there are $25$ swans, so $75$ non-swans, of which $30$ are geese. $\frac{30}{75}=\frac25=40\%$.

**Answer: (C) 40**

amc10-2011-10a-08.title: Ratio of percents
amc10-2011-10a-08.body:
Non-swans make up $100\%-25\%=75\%$ of the birds. The fraction of them that are geese is $\frac{30\%}{75\%}=0.4=40\%$.

**Answer: (C) 40**

amc10-2011-10a-09.title: Width times height
amc10-2011-10a-09.body:
The height runs from $y=-b$ to $y=a$: $a+b$. The width runs from $x=-c$ to $x=d$: $c+d$. Area $=(a+b)(c+d)=ac+ad+bc+bd$.

**Answer: (A)**

amc10-2011-10a-09.title: Test numbers
amc10-2011-10a-09.body:
Take $a=b=c=d=1$: the rectangle is $2\times 2$ with area $4$. Choices (B)–(E) all give $0$; only (A) gives $4$.

**Answer: (A)**

amc10-2011-10a-10.title: Factor 1771
amc10-2011-10a-10.body:
Let $s$ students each buy $p$ pencils at $c$ cents each. Then $s\cdot p\cdot c = 1771 = 7\cdot 11\cdot 23$.

- A majority means $16\le s\le 30$, so $s=23$ (no other product of these primes lies in that range).
- Then $p\cdot c = 77$ with $1<p<c$, so $p=7$, $c=11$.

**Answer: (B) 11**

amc10-2011-10a-10.title: Test the choices
amc10-2011-10a-10.body:
$1771=7\cdot11\cdot23$. If $c=7$, then $sp=253=11\cdot 23$ and $p$ would have to be less than $7$ and bigger than $1$ — impossible. If $c=11$, $sp=161=7\cdot 23$: $s=23$, $p=7<11$ works. (Larger $c$ such as $23$ would force $s\le 11$, not a majority.)

**Answer: (B) 11**

amc10-2011-10a-11.title: Pythagoras on a corner triangle
amc10-2011-10a-11.body:
Let $EB=1$, $AE=7$, so $ABCD$ has side $8$ and area $64$. By symmetry each vertex of $EFGH$ cuts its side into pieces $7$ and $1$, so the corner triangle at $B$ has legs $1$ and $7$. Then $EF^2 = 1^2+7^2=50$. Ratio: $\frac{50}{64}=\frac{25}{32}$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac{25}{32}$**

amc10-2011-10a-11.title: Subtract four corners
amc10-2011-10a-11.body:
The four corner triangles are congruent with legs $1$ and $7$, total area $4\cdot\frac{7}{2}=14$. So $[EFGH] = 64-14=50$ and the ratio is $\frac{50}{64}=\frac{25}{32}$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac{25}{32}$**

amc10-2011-10a-12.title: Set up equations
amc10-2011-10a-12.body:
Let $t$ be the number of two-pointers. Two-pointers give $2t$ points, three-pointers also give $2t$ points, and free throws give $t+1$ points. So $2t+2t+t+1=61$, giving $t=12$ and $t+1=13$ free throws.

**Answer: (A) 13**

amc10-2011-10a-12.title: Test the choices
amc10-2011-10a-12.body:
If there are $f$ free throws, there are $f-1$ two-pointers and the total is $2(f-1)+2(f-1)+f = 5f-4$. Setting $5f-4=61$ gives $f=13$. (Check: $12$ two-pointers $=24$ points, $8$ three-pointers $=24$ points, $13$ free throws: $24+24+13=61$.)

**Answer: (A) 13**

amc10-2011-10a-13.title: Case on the hundreds digit
amc10-2011-10a-13.body:
The hundreds digit must be $2$ or $5$ (the only allowed digits from $2$ to $6$). The units digit must be even: $2$ or $8$.

- Hundreds digit $2$: units digit must be $8$; the tens digit is any of the $4$ unused digits: $4$ numbers.
- Hundreds digit $5$: units digit $2$ or $8$; then $4$ choices for the tens digit: $8$ numbers.

Total $4+8=12$.

**Answer: (A) 12**

amc10-2011-10a-13.title: Choose the units digit first
amc10-2011-10a-13.body:
Units digit $2$: hundreds digit must be $5$, tens digit $4$ choices: $4$. Units digit $8$: hundreds digit $2$ or $5$, tens digit $4$ choices: $8$. Total $12$.

**Answer: (A) 12**

amc10-2011-10a-14.title: Find the condition on the diameter
amc10-2011-10a-14.body:
For diameter $d$: area $\frac{\pi d^2}{4}$, circumference $\pi d$. We need $\frac{\pi d^2}{4}<\pi d$, i.e. $d<4$. So the sum must be $2$ or $3$: outcomes $(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)$, which is $3$ of $36$. Probability $\frac{3}{36}=\frac1{12}$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac{1}{12}$**

amc10-2011-10a-14.title: Using the radius
amc10-2011-10a-14.body:
With radius $r$: $\pi r^2<2\pi r \iff r<2 \iff d<4$. Same count: $\frac{3}{36}=\frac1{12}$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac{1}{12}$**

amc10-2011-10a-15.title: Equation for the trip length
amc10-2011-10a-15.body:
Let the trip be $d$ miles. Gas used: $0.02(d-40)$ gallons. Then $\frac{d}{0.02(d-40)}=55$, so $d = 1.1(d-40)=1.1d-44$, giving $0.1d=44$ and $d=440$.

**Answer: (C) 440**

amc10-2011-10a-15.title: Check a choice
amc10-2011-10a-15.body:
For $440$ miles: gas is used for $400$ miles, $0.02\cdot400=8$ gallons. $440/8 = 55$ miles per gallon. ✓

**Answer: (C) 440**

amc10-2011-10a-16.title: Square the sum
amc10-2011-10a-16.body:
Let $S$ be the sum. Then
$$S^2 = (9-6\sqrt2)+(9+6\sqrt2)+2\sqrt{(9-6\sqrt2)(9+6\sqrt2)} = 18+2\sqrt{81-72}=18+6=24.$$
Since $S>0$, $S=\sqrt{24}=2\sqrt6$.

**Answer: (B) $2\sqrt6$**

amc10-2011-10a-17.title: The sequence repeats
amc10-2011-10a-17.body:
From $A+B+C=B+C+D$ we get $A=D$; similarly $B=E$, $C=F$, $D=G$, $E=H$. So the sequence is $A,B,5,A,B,5,A,B$ and $H=B$. Since $A+B+5=30$, $A+H=A+B=25$.

**Answer: (C) 25**

amc10-2011-10a-17.title: Add cleverly
amc10-2011-10a-17.body:
$(A+B+C)+(C+D+E)+(F+G+H) = 90$ counts every term once except $C$ twice, so the total of all eight terms is $90-5=85$. Also total $= A+(B+C+D)+(E+F+G)+H = A+H+60$. So $A+H=25$.

**Answer: (C) 25**

amc10-2011-10a-18.title: Subtract the overlaps
amc10-2011-10a-18.body:
Put the centers at $A=(-1,0)$, $B=(1,0)$; they touch at the origin $M$, the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$. Circle $C$ is tangent to $\overline{AB}$ at $M$, so its center is $(0,1)$.

Circles $A$ and $C$ have centers $\sqrt2$ apart and meet at $(0,0)$ and $(-1,1)$; the two intersection points and the centers form a unit square. The overlap is two circular segments, each a quarter circle minus a right triangle: $2\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac12\right)=\frac\pi2-1$. The same for circle $B$.

Area of $C$ outside $A$ and $B$: $\pi - 2\left(\frac\pi2-1\right)=2$.

**Answer: (C) 2**

amc10-2011-10a-18.title: Rectangle plus half disk
amc10-2011-10a-18.body:
Use the same coordinates. Split the region by the line $y=1$.

- Above $y=1$: the upper half of circle $C$, which misses $A$ and $B$ entirely. Area $\frac\pi2$.
- Below $y=1$: the lower half of $C$ lies in the rectangle $[-1,1]\times[0,1]$. In that rectangle, the parts not in $A$ or $B$ are the rectangle minus two quarter circles, area $2-\frac\pi2$, and all of it lies inside $C$ (in the unit square with opposite corners at the centers of $A$ and $C$, a point farther than $1$ from one corner is closer than $1$ to the other). So this part has area $2-\frac\pi2$.

Total: $\frac\pi2+2-\frac\pi2=2$.

**Answer: (C) 2**

amc10-2011-10a-19.title: Use the last condition too
amc10-2011-10a-19.body:
$r^2-p^2=300$ with $r^2$ the 2011 population. Factor pairs of $300$ with the same parity: $(2,150),(6,50),(10,30)$, giving $p=74, 22, 10$. Check $p^2+141$ is a square: only $p=22$ works ($484+141=625=25^2$; $74^2+141=5617$ and $10^2+141=241$ are not squares). Growth $300/484\approx0.62$.

**Answer: (E) 62%**

amc10-2011-10a-20.title: Chord of length r spans 60°
amc10-2011-10a-20.body:
A chord of length $r$ together with two radii forms an equilateral triangle, so it cuts off a $60^\circ$ arc. Fix the first point $P$; its chord covers the arc from $P$ to $60^\circ$ clockwise. The second chord meets the first exactly when the second point lies within $60^\circ$ of $P$ on either side (counterclockwise: its chord reaches over $P$; clockwise: it starts on the first arc). That is $120^\circ$ out of $360^\circ$: probability $\frac13$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac{1}{3}$**

amc10-2011-10a-20.title: Arc lengths
amc10-2011-10a-20.body:
Measure the angle $\theta$ from the first point to the second clockwise, uniform on $[0^\circ,360^\circ)$. The two $60^\circ$ arcs overlap iff $\theta<60^\circ$ or $\theta>300^\circ$, total $120^\circ$, probability $\frac{120}{360}=\frac13$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac{1}{3}$**

amc10-2011-10a-21.title: Count equal-weight outcomes
amc10-2011-10a-21.body:
Two pairs have equal weight only if both are genuine–genuine, or both are genuine–counterfeit (a pair of two counterfeits can't be matched, since only two exist).

- Both pairs genuine: $\binom82\binom62=28\cdot15=420$ ways.
- Each pair has one counterfeit: first pair $2\cdot 8=16$ ways, second pair $1\cdot7=7$ ways: $112$.

Conditional probability: $\frac{420}{420+112}=\frac{420}{532}=\frac{15}{19}$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac{15}{19}$**

amc10-2011-10a-22.title: The diagonals form a 5-cycle
amc10-2011-10a-22.body:
The diagonals are $AC, CE, EB, BD, DA$: a closed loop $A\to C\to E\to B\to D\to A$. So we need to color a 5-cycle with adjacent vertices different. Go around: $A$: $6$ choices, $C$: $5$, $E$: $5$, $B$: $5$. For $D$ (adjacent to $B$ and $A$):

- If $A$ and $B$ have the same color, $D$ has $5$ choices.
- Otherwise $D$ has $4$ choices.

Count colorings of $A,C,E,B$ with $B=A$: $6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot1=120$ ($E$ must avoid $C$ and $A$'s color). With $B\ne A$: $6\cdot5\cdot5\cdot5-120=630$. Total: $120\cdot5+630\cdot4=600+2520=3120$.

**Answer: (C) 3120**

amc10-2011-10a-22.title: Chromatic polynomial of a cycle
amc10-2011-10a-22.body:
The number of proper colorings of an $n$-cycle with $k$ colors is $(k-1)^n+(-1)^n(k-1)$. With $n=5$, $k=6$: $5^5-5=3125-5=3120$.

**Answer: (C) 3120**

amc10-2011-10a-23.title: Track the skipped lists
amc10-2011-10a-23.body:
Alice skips $2,5,8,\dots$ (start $2$, step $3$). Barbara's list is that sequence; she skips every middle one: the 2nd, 5th, … terms, i.e. $5, 14, 23,\dots$ (start $5$, step $9$). Each time the start increases by the old step and the step triples:

- Candice gets start $5$, step $9$; skips start $14$, step $27$.
- Debbie: start $14$; skips start $41$, step $81$.
- Eliza: start $41$; skips start $122$, step $243$.
- Fatima: start $122$; skips start $365$, step $729$.

The only number $\le1000$ in the last list is $365$ ($365+729>1000$). George says $365$.

**Answer: (C) 365**

amc10-2011-10a-23.title: Formula
amc10-2011-10a-23.body:
The $k$-th skipped list starts at $1+3+9+\dots+3^{k-1}+1=\frac{3^k+1}{2}$. After six students, George's number is $\frac{3^6+1}{2}=\frac{730}{2}=365$.

**Answer: (C) 365**

amc10-2011-10a-24.title: The intersection is an octahedron
amc10-2011-10a-24.body:
Each regular tetrahedron uses four alternate cube vertices; its edges are face diagonals. The two tetrahedra's edges cross at the centers of the six faces, and the intersection is the regular octahedron with vertices at the six face centers.

That octahedron is two square pyramids with base the middle cross-section square (vertices at the centers of four faces, side $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$, area $\frac12$) and height $\frac12$. Volume $=2\cdot\frac13\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac16$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac16$**

amc10-2011-10a-24.title: Cut corners off one tetrahedron
amc10-2011-10a-24.body:
One tetrahedron has volume $1-4\cdot\frac16=\frac13$ (the cube minus four corner pyramids). The second tetrahedron cuts off a small tetrahedron at each of the first one's four vertices, each similar with ratio $\frac12$, volume $\frac13\cdot\frac18=\frac1{24}$. What's left: $\frac13-4\cdot\frac{1}{24}=\frac16$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac16$**

amc10-2011-10a-25.title: Describe the n-ray partitional points
amc10-2011-10a-25.body:
Take $R$ to be the unit square $[0,1]^2$ and $X=(x,y)$. Every region must be a triangle, so a ray must go to each of the four corners. The triangles on the left side all have apex $X$ and height $x$, so together they have area $\frac x2$; if there are $a$ of them, $\frac{x}{2}=\frac an$, i.e. $x=\frac{2a}{n}$. Similarly $y=\frac{2b}{n}$; the right and top sides then get $\frac n2-a$ and $\frac n2-b$ triangles, so $n$ must be even and $1\le a,b\le \frac n2-1$. Conversely such points work (split each side into equal pieces).

- $100$-ray partitional: $x,y\in\{\frac1{50},\dots,\frac{49}{50}\}$: $49^2=2401$ points.
- Also $60$-ray partitional: $x,y$ must also be multiples of $\frac1{30}$, i.e. multiples of $\frac1{10}$: $9^2=81$ points.

Answer: $2401-81=2320$.

**Answer: (C) 2320**

amc10-2011-10a-25.title: Count with gcd
amc10-2011-10a-25.body:
The grid $\frac{k}{50}$ and the grid $\frac{k}{30}$ share exactly the multiples of $\frac{1}{\gcd(50,30)}=\frac1{10}$. Inside the square: $49$ values per coordinate for the first grid and $9$ common values, so $49^2-9^2=(49-9)(49+9)=40\cdot58=2320$.

**Answer: (C) 2320**
